title: We've been transatlantic pen pals for 70 years and are now more like sisters
content:
We've been transatlantic pen pals for 70 years and are now more like sisters
- Published
Two women who became transatlantic pen pals when they were in the Brownies say they now feel "more like family", having written to each other regularly for 70 years.
Kathleen Bonthron (now Wilson) from Drumchapel in Glasgow was 10 when her group leader gave her the Wisconsin address for 11-year-old Shirley Hedtke (now Yaeger) in 1956.
The pair - now 80 and 81 - began writing to each other and soon built up a rapport, with regular letters going back and forth between Scotland and the United States.
The girls kept in touch throughout their childhood, then their teenage years, and as they settled down and had families - and are still in contact now they are pensioners.
In the 50s, the only way they could communicate was by writing letters through air mail but this later progressed to emails and now their method of choice is WhatsApp.
The bond between the two women is so strong that 55 years ago Kathleen named her daughter after Shirley. They are now known in their families as Shirley America and Shirley Scotland.
"When Shirley was born, as I had a friend in America I just thought we'll have Shirley," Kathleen said. "And her dad was quite happy with that.
"Shirley was chuffed to bits."
Her daughter Shirley added: "Shirley has actually gifted me her childhood mug with her name on it."
Speaking from her home in Wisconsin, Shirley (America) said: "My mother named me after Shirley Temple and I was so honoured that Shirley was named after me. It was just wonderful, especially once I met her."
Shirley, a former nurse, recalled being given Kathleen's address in 1956.
"My Brownie leader came in with a cigar box full of names and asked if anyone would like a pen pal from Scotland," she said. "I grabbed a name and it was Kathleen Bonthron.
"We just wrote a few times a year at first but then we started writing more and it just got to be fun.
"I got to learn about her culture and she learned about ours. And I learned new words. I loved her from the minute I started writing to her.
"We told each other about our families, Brownies and school and then later, of course, we got into the dating which was exciting."
Kathleen, who now lives in Lenzie, said: "You didn't know what America was at that age. I think we just used to write about school and going out with our mums and dads.
"It was just all chit chat, as it is now. It's just bigger chit chat now."
What was happening in 1956 when Kathleen and Shirley became pen pals?
Worldwide:
- The Suez Crisis - Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal, threatening British shipping and economic interests, leading to British and French forces invading Egypt to retake the canal, alongside Israel. Facing severe financial pressure and opposition from the US, British troops withdrew in defeat
In the USA:
- Rock 'n' roll is on the rise with Elvis Presley releasing Heartbreak Hotel and Bill Haley and His Comets starring in Rock Around the Clock
- The US Supreme Court ruled that Alabama laws requiring segregated buses were unconstitutional, officially ending a historic boycott
- Hollywood star Marilyn Monroe married playwright Arthur Miller in New York
In the UK:
- Queen Elizabeth II opened the world's first full-scale commercial nuclear power station at Calder Hall in Cumberland
- The Duke of Edinburgh's Award was launched to help young people build life skills
- The beginnings of homegrown rock and pop, with artists like Tommy Steele beginning to chart, while Skiffle bands inspired teenagers to pick up washboards and tea chest basses
In Scotland:
- Dundee Corporation Tramways and Edinburgh Corporation Tramways operated their final tram services, ending an era of streetcar transit in those cities
- The National Library of Scotland opened its first purpose-built premises on George IV Bridge in Edinburgh
- Scotland's first commercial ski centre opened in Glencoe
Kathleen and Shirley have met three times - twice in Scotland in 2007 and 2019 and then once in the US a few weeks ago.
"The first time we met, Shirley was just what she is," Kathleen said. "She's as friendly as me and can talk. We both can talk.
"It just felt natural. We just slotted right in with each other.
"I'm quite happy now that I've seen her in her house. I feel a bit closer to her, she's more like family now.
"But we don't stop talking. We do not stop talking. We never get to the end of the stories because we're talking so much.
"We will never not be in touch."
'She's like a sister to me'
Kathleen, who was formerly a punch card operator at IBM and then a doctor's receptionist, added: "She's just a good friend now, more like family. I mean, it's been 70 years. We speak on the phone every now and then but mostly message on WhatsApp."
Shirley said: "When we were in Scotland we only got to see Kathleen for a few hours because we had a schedule but when they came to the US we lived together and really got to know each other.
"It was just wonderful. She's like a sister to me. We have discussed everything - our pregnancies, our kids when they were little - she was always there for me."
Both women have a son and a daughter.
As well as Shirley, Kathleen had her son Andrew with her late husband Eric and now has two grandchildren.
Shirley has been married to Daniel for 61 years and has a daughter Christine and son Jon.
And now the women's children have vowed to keep in touch with each other.
"The plan is for Christine - Shirley's daughter - and I, to keep in touch," Shirley (Scotland) said. "So we can be the next pen pals."
Shirley (America) said: "I'm so glad. My daughter has heard about Kathleen's family her whole life and when they met they hit it off right away."
Speaking about her friendship with Kathleen, she added: "Kathleen is always such a happy person. She was such a great pen pal to have.
"None of my friends kept up with their pen pals. We were the only ones."

title: Į Panevėžį grįžo kino centras „Garsas“: žadama naujovė – slapti kino seansai
content:
Į Panevėžio miesto centrą grįžęs kino centras „Garsas“ pradeda naują etapą. Čia ir toliau bus didelis dėmesys skiriamas nekomerciniam bei autoriniam kinui, plečiama edukacinė veikla – žiūrovai mokysis suprasti ir interpretuoti filmą.
2021-ųjų kovą Panevėžio centre pradėtas griauti kino centro „Garsas“ pastatas. Griovimo darbai atidėlioti ne kartą dėl visuomenininkų pasipriešinimo vietoje šio pastato statyti Stasio Eidrigevičiaus menų centrą.
Nepaisant pasipriešinimų, beveik 4000 kvadratinių metrų „Garso“ pastatas nugriautas, jo vietoje duris atvėrė „Stasys museum“. Po atidarymo praėjus dvejiems metams į senąją vietą grįžo ir kino centras „Garsas“, tapęs muziejaus padaliniu. Žiūrovai ir toliau galės žiūrėti nekomercinį kiną, tik jau naujose patalpose.
„Viena tokia iš „Garso“ krypčių, kurią paryškiname sugrįždami iš naujo, tai dėmesio atkreipimas į pasaulio kiną, kas anksčiau galbūt „Garsui“ buvo labiau akcentuojamas Europos autorinis kinas. Dabar mes norime atkreipti dėmesį, kad autorinis kinas iš viso pasaulio bus rodomas“, – sako „Garso“ vadovė Ignė Smilingytė.
Pasak „Garso“ vadovės, repertuare dažniau bus rodoma kino klasika, restauruoti filmai, specialūs seansai skirtingoms auditorijoms.
„Panevėžio žiūrovai yra gan smalsūs ir jie nori kalbėti apie kiną. Kino centras „Garsas“ visada siūlė daug renginių su diskusijomis, su pristatymais, tai šitą stiprinsim dar labiau. Ruošiame ir festivalio naują idėją, kuris ir bus paremtas diskusijų, augimo kartu su kinu formatu“, – teigia I. Smilingytė.
Bus atnaujinta, sustiprinta kino edukacijos kryptis. „Garso kino mokykla“ ir toliau ruoš Panevėžio ir aplinkinio regiono moksleivius kino studijoms.
„Turėsime ir tokią gana stiprią kryptį, daugiau tokių potyriminių dirbtuvių formato veiklų. Dirbsime ir su kino garsu, ir su analoginiu kinu, kas yra kino juosta, piešime ant kino juostos ir animuosime ją, o po to gyvai žiūrėsime iš analoginio kino projektoriaus“, – pasakoja „Garso“ kino edukacijų koordinatorė Miglė Križinauskaitė.
Kino centras „Garsas“ pristato ir visišką naujovę – slaptus kino seansus. Tai reiškia, žiūrovai bus kviečiami į filmą, kurio pavadinimas nebus iš anksto skelbiamas.

title: QC-sponsored orphans sweep top three places in Qur’an competition
content:
Somalia’s Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre has hailed three Qatar Charity (QC)-sponsored Somali orphans after they swept the top three places in the international “Rofaqa” category of the Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed bin Thani Qur’an Competition.
He also praised the QC’s longstanding support for orphan care and education in Somalia.
The event, held recently in Qatar, drew hundreds of orphaned contestants from around the world.
The prime minister made the remarks while receiving the winners at his office in Mogadishu.
Competing in the full Qur'an memorisation category, Abdulghani Abdulqadir Sheikh Hussein claimed first place, Abdulrahman Qasim Mohammed took second, and Abdulrahman Ahmed Mahmoud secured third.
Barre commended Qatar Charity for combining orphan care with education and empowerment, helping young people excel academically and in Qur'anic studies.
He said the students’ success underscores the respected status of Qur'an memorisers in Somali society and highlights the country’s promising talent in Islamic and Qur'anic studies.
Describing the clean sweep as “a source of pride for the Somali people”, the prime minister urged the winners to continue memorising and teaching the Qur'an and promoting its values in their communities.
He also announced that the three winners would receive free education under the same support granted to the country’s top performers in the national secondary school certificate examinations.
He told them: “The government is proud of you for winning first, second, and third places in this international competition. Your achievement is an honour for all Somalis, and I will direct the ministry of education to provide you with free education in support of your academic journey.”
The winners were among 389 contestants from 20 countries who entered the international “Rofaqa” competition for orphans, organised by the QC in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Endowments (Awqaf) and Islamic Affairs.
A select group advanced to the final round.
The “Rofaqa” category is the Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed bin Thani Qur'an Competition’s first international category dedicated to orphans sponsored by Qatar Charity.
Open to participants aged 12-20, it offers a competitive Qur'an memorisation platform within an educational setting that combines Qur'anic excellence with humanitarian care.
Somalia’s ambassador to Qatar Dr Mohammed Ahmed Sheikh Ali also congratulated the winners, saying that their clean sweep reflected the value of investing in people.
He said the result showed how sustained care, education, and training can turn talent into achievement.

title: 'Our industry is still male dominated, but things are changing'
content:
'Our industry is still male dominated, but things are changing'
- Published
There has been a significant increase in the number of women studying for engineering degrees in Northern Ireland, new figures show.
Over the last 10 years the number of female students studying Mechanical Engineering at Queen's University has increased by 40%, while at Ulster University the number studying engineering has almost doubled over the past decade.
But employment figures also show that the engineering and wider manufacturing industries in Northern Ireland are still male dominated.
Now a group of women working in the engineering industry in Mid Ulster are raising awareness about the opportunities for women in the sector.
Lorraine O'Neill is one of them.
When she first joined one of County Tyrone's largest manufacturing firms back in 1994, there were less than 10 women working there. Now the company employs more than 300 females across Northern Ireland.
"Yes there are still gender stereotypes in this industry, but we've come a long way since I first started out", she said.
"When I joined more than 30 years ago, there were no females in the senior management team at all, but today 50% of our senior leadership team are female."
O'Neill is currently Senior Logistics Manager at Powerscreen, a global manufacturer of equipment used in the quarrying, mining and construction industries.
She wants to encourage more women to aim for senior leadership roles in manufacturing and engineering sector.
She said: "I love my job, I help ship our machinery all over the world and no day is the same.
"A lot of people have a picture in their head about engineering and manufacturing jobs but they don't understand there are so many different opportunities from logistics, to finance to procurement.
She added: "Things are changing and seeing women in senior roles really helps."
Tyrone is known for its cluster of engineering and manufacturing firms and today more than 40% of the world's mobile crushing and screening equipment is made in the Mid Ulster area.
Founded as Ulster Plant Ltd in 1966, Powerscreen pioneered the concept of mobile screening.
Over the following decades, the business grew from a local engineering firm into a global brand. It was acquired by Terex Corporation in 1999 but continued to retain its roots in County Tyrone.
As it celebrates its 60th year in business, together with its parent company Terex, they are looking at how their workforce has changed and diversified.
Recent graduate Sneha Saji has been working at Powerscreen as a manufacturing engineer for a number of months.
She said: "Before starting my engineering degree, I probably did have an idea in my head that this industry was primarily for men, but doing internships and seeing women in senior engineering roles really did inspire me.
"It can be daunting if you're in certain departments that might be male dominated, but I would say just give it a shot, don't let the stereotypes put you off, ask plenty of questions and don't be afraid to make mistakes."
Amelia McCormack has been with Powerscreen for seven years and now works as a senior logistics co-ordinator.
She joined the company through an apprenticeship.
The "earn while you learn" element attracted her and she has "never looked back".
She said it is a "hands on, fast paced" job.
"I am really proud to be a woman working in this industry, showing that things have changed, but it's fair to say that there is still work to do."
Figures show that women hold approximately 11% of engineering roles in Northern Ireland and make up about 23% of its manufacturing workforce.
Juliana Early is a professor at the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at Queen's University.
She believes the increase of women studying Engineering centred degrees is a sign that things are changing.
She said: "Having worked at Queen's for the past 23 years, I have seen first-hand the sustained commitment to increasing participation of women in the engineering sector.
"This growth reflects changing perceptions of the opportunities afforded by engineering and the success of targeted efforts to ensure that talented women see the sector as a place where they can thrive."
'I never let stereotypes put me off'
Rachel Pattison has worked as an engineer in Northern Ireland for 16 years.
She believes the key to more gender diversity is getting young women interested in science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) at an early age.
She said: "I was always good at maths and physics at school and had very supportive parents, so I never thought that engineering and manufacturing was something that I wouldn't be able to do."
Pattison credits that to being surrounded by encouraging teachers and because of that the idea that it might be a male-centred workforce was not off-putting.
In 2024, while maths and physics were among the most popular subjects studied at A-level by boys they were not in the top five most popular subjects taken by girls.
According to the Department for the Economy's (DfE) women in STEM taskforce, only one in five STEM jobs are filled by women in Northern Ireland.
Pattison is now head of operations for Tierco Healthcare, a company that designs specialists seats for hospitals and care facilities.
She believes changing perceptions for young women will continue to impact the statistics.
"There's no arguing the employment statistics show there's still along way to go in terms of female representation in the industry, but it's about shining a light on those women already working it.
"To any young women out there who want to break into the industry, I would just say be curious, if it's something you feel passionate about do not let anybody pigeonhole you or say you can't make it, because it's not true."

title: In an outback town, this small venue raised $1 million to save itself
content:
Live music fans raise $1m to save beloved Alice Springs venue after landlord flags sale
It might seem unlikely that a volunteer-run venue in one of the country's most remote towns could inspire people from across Australia and the world to help raise $1 million to save it.
But it did.
Over the past month, the founders of popular Alice Springs live music venue The Black Wreath have been fundraising to buy the building and turn the whole block into a creative hub after their landlord put the property up for sale.
Artists and music industry figures came on board, including Amyl and the Sniffers, who played at The Black Wreath's Blacken Open Air festival in 2022, as well as donors who matched pledges dollar for dollar.
The Black Wreath hosts local gigs and offers artists a recording and rehearsal space, helping kick-start the careers of some of the most remote bands in the world.
Before he launched the campaign on August 4, the Black Wreath's founder, who goes by the mononym Pirate, hardly used social media.
But by the end of the appeal, he was posting daily videos, pushing as hard as he could to save one of the creative heartbeats of Alice Springs.
"It's a massive milestone, I'm really proud of the community achievement and everyone that's gotten behind this," he said.
The fundraisers gave themselves until September 13 to reach their $1 million funding goal, but hit the target two days early before a massive weekend of coordinated gigs across the country in solidarity with the cause.
It wasn't until the day after the Alice Springs gig, headlined by South East Desert Metal, that Pirate had his first day off in months.
He said the whole town "became a metal head for the night".
"The last month it's been 12 to 15 hours every single day, it hasn't been healthy, but it's been necessary," Pirate said.
"And yesterday I just absolutely collapsed, couldn't do a bloody thing."
However, Pirate said there was a long road still ahead.
As part of the fundraising campaign, people from across the country made pledges for something in return, which ranged from T-shirts, records, rings and hats to an entire festival, Blacken Open Air, to be held on April 30 next year.
"I'm not celebrating yet just yet; I'm getting back to work," Pirate said.
Loading..."It's just the beginning of the process, we've raised some money and now we need to negotiate with the owners.
"There's a lot more to do."
Pirate said the grand vision was to turn the entire property into a creative precinct.
"My big hopes and aspirations and dreams are that it's run as a foundation and the income generated goes into local music and arts," he said.
"And touring Central Australian artists outside of here, [as well as] bringing artists to Alice Springs and putting them on stages here as well.
"Fifteen years of doing this, I find that the travel aspect has been the biggest hindrance to connecting us with a wider community."
Ltyentye Apurta/Santa Teresa musicians South East Desert Metal describe themselves as the most isolated touring band in the world, and credit The Black Wreath for success that's seen them perform on the steps of the Sydney Opera House.
The band's lead vocalist and guitarist, Chris Wallace, said there was nothing else like it in Alice Springs.
"I really love it, all that comes from Black Wreath," he said.
"Black Wreath was the one that found us, and made us who we are."
Reflecting on the successful fundraiser, Pirate said it was "an amazing moment for the whole nation, especially for the heavy metal community".
"This is very historic," he said.
"I'm proud to be a part of that community and we're as far away from everyone as you can possibly get, but right now it feels like there's no distance at all between us."

title: A Country Is More Than Its Politics. It’s What It Builds to Last
content:
A Country Is More Than Its Politics. It’s What It Builds to Last
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — Ethiopia’s political future is increasingly being framed around a question larger than the contest for power: whether a country with deep historical, social and political differences can build enough common ground to make peace, development and national cohesion enduring rather than temporary.
That question gives particular weight to the ideas of national consensus, reconciliation and Medemer that have increasingly shaped Ethiopia’s political discourse in recent years. Medemer, presented by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed as a philosophy of synergy and collective progress, seeks to place cooperation, shared national purpose and the pooling of national strengths at the center of Ethiopia’s political and development trajectory. In the government’s formulation, the philosophy has also been developed into a broader concept of the “Medemer State,” intended to give institutional expression to those principles.
At its core is a proposition with direct political consequences: Ethiopia’s differences do not have to be settled through the permanent defeat of one side by another. They can instead become subjects of negotiation, compromise and common purpose.
That proposition matters in a country whose political history has repeatedly demonstrated the costs of unresolved differences. For decades, competing visions of statehood, identity, power and national interest have frequently been expressed through confrontation. The challenge now is whether political disagreement can increasingly be made a contest of ideas, programmes and arguments rather than a contest of force.
This is the political significance of the National Dialogue.
The process that culminated in August brought nearly 4,000 Ethiopians from different political, social and professional backgrounds together for 40 days of deliberation. Eight broad areas were placed on the table, ranging from nation-building, state structure and political systems to historical grievances, reconciliation, human rights, socio-economic issues, good governance and peacebuilding. The deliberations produced about 400 recommendations.
Its importance, however, lies less in the size of the conference than in the political method it sought to advance.
Participants with sharply different perspectives were required to sit in the same national forum, listen to competing positions and search for areas of agreement. The National Dialogue Commission said the process was intended to create a foundation for addressing deep-rooted disagreements through consultation rather than force.
That distinction goes to the heart of Ethiopia’s search for a new political culture.
A political system cannot build lasting national cohesion if every disagreement becomes an existential confrontation. Nor can a country continually rebuild its political order around the victor and the vanquished. A durable national consensus requires a different premise: political competitors can disagree profoundly while remaining participants in the same national project.
The idea is closely connected to the notion of a common national narrative—not a demand that every Ethiopian hold identical views about history or politics, but an effort to establish a broader sense of shared belonging, shared interests and shared destiny. A country of Ethiopia’s scale and diversity cannot be held together by political uniformity. Its cohesion has to come from a national framework in which differences have legitimate space but do not automatically become grounds for permanent separation.
This is where reconciliation becomes more than a political slogan.
Reconciliation is difficult precisely because it asks politics to move beyond the immediate satisfaction of victory. It requires acknowledging that yesterday’s adversary may still be part of tomorrow’s national community. It also requires political institutions to create space for people and groups once separated by conflict to return to political and civic life.
The government’s New Year clemency for hundreds of prisoners, announced as Ethiopia entered 2019, provided a recent practical expression of that approach. The measure was presented in connection with reconciliation and calls emerging from the national consultation process. More than 600 federal prisoners, including prominent figures, were released around the New Year.
Clemency does not, by itself, resolve political disagreements or erase the grievances behind them. But the political meaning attached to such measures is significant: reconciliation requires openings through which former opponents can move from confrontation toward participation.
Ethiopia’s recent political messaging has also drawn a sharper line between the politics of the gun and the politics of ideas. Prime Minister Abiy has argued that the era of resolving political differences through force should give way to an inclusive political landscape in which disagreements are addressed through peaceful political engagement.
That is a consequential standard for Ethiopia’s political future.
The alternative is familiar: political disagreement becomes militarized; political competition becomes existential; grievances become recruitment tools; and every generation inherits unfinished conflicts from the previous one.
The other path is harder but fundamentally different. It asks political actors to compete with arguments rather than weapons, organize around ideas rather than violence, and accept that political change can be pursued through institutions, elections, dialogue, public debate and the written word.
In that sense, the image of computers, cellphones and pens instead of guns captures more than technological modernization. It describes a desired transformation in the means through which a society conducts its political life.
The cellphone has become a platform for political expression. The computer has become a tool for organizing knowledge, communicating ideas and connecting citizens. The pen remains a symbol of argument, persuasion and intellectual contest. None of these eliminates political conflict. They change the instruments through which conflict can be expressed.
For a young and increasingly connected Ethiopian population, that distinction is particularly important. Political energy does not have to disappear; it can be redirected. Competition does not have to disappear; it can become competition over ideas, policies and national priorities.
This is also where Medemer intersects with the broader question of Ethiopia’s future. The philosophy has been presented not simply as a call for political reconciliation but as a framework for combining national capacities that are otherwise fragmented—social, economic, political and institutional strengths brought together toward shared objectives. The government has increasingly linked the concept to national unity, sovereignty, prosperity and collective development.
Its political test, therefore, is not whether the word itself becomes universally accepted. The more consequential question is whether the underlying principle—addition rather than destruction, cooperation without eliminating competition, and national purpose without denying diversity—can become part of Ethiopia’s political practice.
The National Dialogue has provided one avenue for testing that principle. Reconciliation measures have provided another. Political reforms, public consultations and efforts to widen participation constitute other parts of the same larger question.
None should be mistaken for a finished process.
National consensus cannot be declared into existence. It has to be built repeatedly through institutions, political conduct and public experience. Reconciliation cannot be completed through a single pardon. It requires the gradual rebuilding of trust between citizens, communities and political actors. And a common national narrative cannot be imposed successfully from above; it becomes durable when people across differences recognize enough of themselves and their aspirations in it.
The stakes extend beyond domestic politics.
A more peaceful and cohesive Ethiopia has implications for the Horn of Africa, where the country’s size, population, economy, diplomatic weight and geographic position give its internal stability a wider regional dimension. Ethiopia’s ability to pursue development, strengthen economic ties, contribute to regional peace and engage the continent from a position of stability is closely connected to its capacity to manage its own political differences peacefully.
That is why Ethiopia’s search for consensus has a continental dimension. A country of more than 135 million people cannot be politically consequential at home without its internal trajectory affecting the wider region. Stability creates room for economic production, regional trade, diplomacy and cooperation; prolonged political fragmentation does the opposite.
The larger ambition, then, is not simply to end one disagreement or close one chapter of political conflict. It is to establish a political culture in which disagreement itself no longer has to threaten the country’s future.
That would mean making room for competing ideas without making enemies of those who hold them; preserving national diversity without allowing it to become permanent political fracture; pursuing reconciliation without forgetting the lessons of conflict; and building consensus without demanding unanimity.
A country is indeed more than its politics. Its political system is only one part of what determines whether its achievements endure.
What ultimately matters is what remains after political arguments have moved on: whether a generation leaves behind greater trust than it inherited, whether former adversaries can participate in the same national life, whether political disagreements can be settled without violence, and whether Ethiopia can convert its enormous human and material potential into a shared national future.
The lasting measure of Ethiopia’s political transformation will therefore not be how forcefully one political narrative defeats another. It will be whether a sufficiently broad national consensus can emerge around a more fundamental proposition: that Ethiopia’s future is large enough to accommodate difference, strong enough to withstand disagreement, and valuable enough to be built through ideas rather than guns.
That is the deeper political question behind Medemer, reconciliation and the National Dialogue—and one that will ultimately be answered not by a single government, conference or political generation, but by the country’s ability to turn the politics of today into the foundations of peace, strength and prosperity for generations to come.

title: UKZN graduates honour family ties and seeds planted by elders
content:
Some 70 years ago a seed was planted in little Dolly Nonthuzelo Nyasulu as she watched with fascination midwives deliver babies and sat with them as they talked about birthing stories.
This week Nyasulu, 82, reaped the fruits when she graduated with a Doctor of Philosophy in Public Health from the University of KwaZulu-Natal looking at a Family-Centred Postnatal Care Approach in rural KwaZulu-Natal.
Her thesis explored the potential of involving families more meaningfully in the care of mothers and newborns, a seed she told the Sunday Times was planted when she was a little girl in Flagstaff in the Eastern Cape.
Proving that age is no barrier to learning and the pursuit of a lifelong dream, the eldest of nine children said she was proud of her achievement.
“I feel incredibly good and very excited,” said Nyasulu.
“I still can’t believe that I have made it to the finish line. It has been such a long journey, with many challenges along the way, so reaching this point feels very special to me.”
Nyasulu’s doctoral study was supervised by Prof Myra Taylor and Dr Nelisiwe Khuzwayo and her research was supported by decades of experience in nursing, midwifery, maternal and newborn health, education and healthcare policy.
Her professional journey began with general nursing, followed by midwifery, psychiatric nursing, advanced midwifery and neonatal nursing. She later completed a Bachelor of Nursing Degree in Community Health Nursing and Nursing Administration and a Clinical Master’s in Nursing specialising in Maternal, Child and Women’s Health.
The grandmother of five and two great-grandchildren also worked as KwaZulu-Natal Provincial Maternal, Child and Women’s Health Coordinator and initiatives focused on maternal and newborn health. She has also contributed to midwifery education, healthcare policy and the development of national and provincial maternal and newborn-care guidelines.
But her passion to enrol in nursing training at Livingstone Hospital in Port Elizabeth in 1964 ― and specialise in midwifery ― was prompted by her experiences of a child where births involved entire families, with relatives participating in different ways to support the mother and the midwife.
“This study feels like a full-circle moment for me,” she said, having spent decades studying and practising midwifery before returning to the importance of family involvement in childbirth and maternal care.
“In the old days the concept of family-centred postnatal care, where family members work collaboratively with healthcare providers, including midwives, to care for mothers and their newborns. Midwives and others in the community were instrumental even before the birth of a baby is born.
“Then with the disintegration of the family unit, with people moving out of the communities and into towns or townships, this ended. However, it continues in countries like Scandinavia and Brazil, the latter which has a traditional element and other places too. I have a vision that we could reintroduce this practice but with collaboration with healthcare providers, the health department and the community.
“I am praying that I have a few more years left to allow me to get this off the ground. Then I think I would have made some meaningful change in this field,” she said.
Her PhD studies were marked by significant personal challenges including the loss of her daughter in 2019 and her husband, Guy, who had been her greatest supporter. She also faced health challenges and had to adapt to the technological demands of postgraduate study.
Yet, with the support of her family and supervisors, she persevered. “In many ways, I feel that I did not walk this journey alone,” she said.
“There were people around me who carried me when I no longer felt I could carry myself.”
Another graduate who felt carried was Bachelor of Law (LLB) graduate Lethukuthula Mngomezulu, whose unusual tie paid tribute to his grandmothers, both of whom are now dead, and he carried them with him as he crossed the graduation stage on Thursday.
“This was my second qualification, but it was my first time walking across the stage because, with my first qualification, it was during Covid-19,” he explained.
Mngomezulu, who has a graphic design company he started while he was studying for his first degree, a Bachelor of Social Science in Criminology, designed the tie.
“At the top is my maternal grandmother, Sibusisiwe MaMsomi-Dlamini and at the bottom, my paternal grandmother, Siphiwe MaSikhakhane-Mngomezulu. The baby is me at 18 months,” he said.
He said both his grandmothers played an instrumental role in his life and education.
“MaMsomi, every year when the year began, she would buy me a set of my school uniform because she believed that I had to look presentable at school, and she always wanted me to do well and thrive academically. MaSikhakhane always motivated me to achieve more in life.
“She always used to say, ‘Imfundo iyona angasoze yakwala noma ungayishela kangakanani,’ meaning education or a qualification is like that one girlfriend that will never leave you or disappoint you, no matter how many times you ask her out.”
Mngomezulu said the graduation coincides with their shared birth month, September.
“I know if they were both still alive, they would be over the moon with joy and excitement.”

title: Wiener Neudorf mit VCÖ-Mobilitätspreis ausgezeichnet
content:
Die Marktgemeinde Wiener Neudorf habe zahlreiche Maßnahmen gesetzt, damit Kinder und Jugendliche sicher, selbstständig und umweltfreundlich mobil sein können, so die Begründung der Fachjury.
Neue Geh- und Radwege, sichere Querungen sowie mehr Abstellplätze für Roller und Fahrräder verbessern laut Verkehrsclub Österreich (VCÖ) die Sicherheit auf Schulwegen. Workshops für Kinder der vierten Volksschulklasse vermitteln zudem den sicheren Umgang mit öffentlichen Verkehrsmitteln, Fahrplänen sowie dem Schulweg zur weiterführenden Schule.
„Was für Kinder funktioniert, hilft auch Menschen mit Kinderwagen oder Rollator. Wenn Kinder gerne gehen, Rad fahren und öffentliche Verkehrsmittel nutzen, wird die Zahl der Elterntaxis reduziert und Kinder und Jugendliche bekommen regelmäßig eine Portion gesunde Bewegung", gratuliert VCÖ-Geschäftsführerin Ulla Rasmussen zum Gewinn der Kategorie „Kindgerechtes Verkehrssystem“.
Insgesamt 13 Projekte ausgezeichnet
Der VCÖ-Mobilitätspreis ist Österreichs größter Wettbewerb für umweltverträgliche Mobilität und nachhaltigen Gütertransport. Heuer wurde er zum 35. Mal vergeben und stand unter dem Motto „nachhaltig.effizient.innovativ“. Insgesamt wurden für den Mobilitätspreis 388 Projekte eingereicht.
Neben dem Konzept „Kinder als Mobilitätsbotschafter" aus Wiener Neudorf wurden noch zwölf weitere Mobilitätsprojekte von Verkehrsminister Peter Hanke (SPÖ), VCÖ und ÖBB ausgezeichnet.

title: Bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy cứu hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ở Phú Quốc
content:
Bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy cứu hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ở Phú Quốc
Hai bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim được bác sĩ Chợ Rẫy phối hợp Bệnh viện Mặt trời Phú Quốc (An Giang) can thiệp tái thông mạch vành kịp thời.
Ngày 20/9, BS.CK2 Lý Ích Trung, Trưởng khoa Tim mạch can thiệp Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, cho biết đây là hai ca can thiệp đầu tiên sau khi hai bệnh viện ký hợp tác chuyên môn hồi tháng 7. Bệnh nhân đầu tiên, 65 tuổi, nhập viện với triệu chứng khó thở, tức ngực, choáng váng, vã mồ hôi, tiền sử hút thuốc lá nhiều. Điện tâm đồ cho thấy bệnh nhân nhồi máu cơ tim ST chênh lên thành dưới.
Bác sĩ Nguyễn Tuấn Anh, Khoa Can thiệp tim mạch Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, vừa được điều động đến Phú Quốc tối hôm trước, phối hợp êkíp địa phương can thiệp cho bệnh nhân. Động mạch vành phải được tái thông thành công, dòng chảy phục hồi tốt, bệnh nhân giảm tức ngực và khó thở.
Ngay sau đó, bệnh viện tiếp nhận người đàn ông 58 tuổi, có tiền sử hút thuốc lá. Ông mệt và khó thở kéo dài, khám sức khỏe phát hiện điện tim bất thường nên được kiểm tra chuyên sâu. Kết quả cho thấy chức năng co bóp thất trái giảm, phân suất tống máu khoảng 45%, người bệnh được chẩn đoán nhồi máu cơ tim bán cấp thành trước, suy tim mức độ 2, rối loạn lipid máu và đái tháo đường. Bác sĩ can thiệp tái thông thành công đoạn động mạch bị tắc, dòng chảy phục hồi tốt.
Theo bác sĩ Trung, nhồi máu cơ tim ST chênh lên là thể có nguy cơ tử vong cao, cần tái thông động mạch vành càng sớm càng tốt. Nếu không được xử trí tại Phú Quốc, người bệnh phải chuyển vào đất liền để can thiệp, kéo dài thêm thời gian cấp cứu. Mỗi giờ chậm trễ can thiệp có thể làm tăng nguy cơ tử vong cho bệnh nhân khoảng 5-10%.
"Thời gian từ khi tiếp nhận đến khi can thiệp càng ngắn thì càng hạn chế vùng cơ tim bị tổn thương và giảm biến chứng", bác sĩ nói. Cả hai bệnh nhân được theo dõi sau can thiệp và vừa xuất viện trong tình trạng ổn định.
Theo BS.CK2 Phạm Thanh Việt, Giám đốc Bệnh viện Chợ Rẫy, chương trình hợp tác với Bệnh viện Mặt trời Phú Quốc nhằm kết nối chuyên môn, hỗ trợ xử trí các ca bệnh phức tạp ngay tại địa phương, đặc biệt là nhồi máu cơ tim cấp và đột quỵ não. Chợ Rẫy đã điều động bác sĩ chuyên khoa đến Phú Quốc, phối hợp với đội ngũ tại chỗ trong cấp cứu và điều trị, hướng đến giảm chuyển bệnh nhân vào đất liền.

title: انتخابات المغرب.. صور الحبر تتحول إلى دعوة للتصويت
content:
انتقلت أجواء الانتخابات التشريعية في المغرب من مراكز الاقتراع إلى منصات التواصل الاجتماعي، حيث نشر ناخبون صور أيديهم بعد الإدلاء بأصواتهم، مرفقة بدعوات للآخرين إلى التوجه إلى صناديق الاقتراع.
ونشر عدد من المصوتين صور الحبر على أصابعهم، مرفقة بعبارة "عطينا الدليل"، في دعوة إلى متابعيهم لإثبات أنهم أدوا واجبهم الوطني.
وشجعت العبارة آخرين على الرد في التعليقات بصور مماثلة بعد الإدلاء بأصواتهم. في تفاعل يشبه التحدي على المنصات الرقمية. وتمنح هذه المنشورات التصويت حضورا خارج مراكز الاقتراع، خصوصا بين مستخدمي المنصات.
من الصورة إلى الدعوة
ولا تعرض المنشورات تجربة التصويت فحسب، بل تسعى أيضا إلى تشجيع الآخرين عليه. فبدلا من الاكتفاء برسالة عامة تدعو إلى المشاركة، يقدم الناخب نفسه مثالا، ثم ينقل الدعوة إلى دائرة أصدقائه ومتابعيه.
وتكتسب هذه الدعوات اهتماما خاصا في النقاش حول مشاركة الشباب، الذين تنشط بينهم المنصات الرقمية، بينما تتباين مواقفهم من الانتخابات والأحزاب.
وقد رصدت تقارير إعلامية، قبيل الاقتراع، شبابا يأملون في التغيير عبر التصويت، وآخرين يشككون في قدرة الأحزاب على الاستجابة لمطالبهم المرتبطة خاصة بالعمل.
وفتحت صناديق الاقتراع أبوابها الأربعاء لاختيار برلمان جديد يفرز حكومة لخمسة أعوام. وبدأ التصويت عند الساعة 8:00 بالتوقيت المحلي على أن يتنهي في السابعة مساء.
ويتنافس أكثر من سبعة آلاف مرشح على أصوات نحو 16 مليون ناخب، من أصل نحو 36 مليون مغربي، لاختيار 395 نائبا.
وأفادت وزارة الداخلية أن نسبة المشاركة في الانتخابات بلغت 11.34 في المئة إلى حدود الساعة 12 زوالا، من مختلف مناطق المملكة.

title: Saccos, vikundi vinavyoleta mageuzi utunzaji akiba nchini
content:
Saccos, vikundi vinavyoleta mageuzi utunzaji akiba nchini
Kwa miaka mingi neno akiba kwa Watanzania wengi limehusishwa zaidi na benki lakini mabadiliko katika mfumo wa huduma za fedha yamepanua mahali ambako mwananchi anaweza kutunza fedha zake.
Kutoka kwenye akaunti za benki hadi Saccos, vikundi vya akiba na huduma za kidijitali, njia za kuhifadhi fedha zimeongezeka na kuifanya dhana ya akiba kuingia zaidi katika maisha ya watu wenye viwango tofauti vya kipato.
Mabadiliko hayo yanaonekana pia katika ukuaji wa Saccos na vikundi vya akiba ambavyo vimekuwa vikitoa njia mbadala kwa wananchi ambao huenda wasitumie benki mara kwa mara au wanaohitaji mfumo unaowawezesha kuweka fedha kwa pamoja na baadaye kupata mikopo.
Hili linatajwa kuchochewa na kuongezeka kwa elimu ya fedha kwa jamii, kujua umuhimu wa kutunza akiba, kukopa ili kuendeleza maisha yao na kuwa katika vikundi vya kuweka na kukopa.
Hiyo ni baada ya takwimu za Ripoti ya Huduma Jumuishi za Fedha Tanzania ya mwaka 2025 ya Benki Kuu ya Tanzania (BoT) kuonyesha kuwa idadi ya akaunti za akiba katika Saccos Tanzania Bara imeongezeka kutoka 1.38 milioni mwaka 2023 hadi 1.55 milioni mwaka 2024 na kufikia 1.57 milioni mwaka 2025.
Wakati ambao thamani ya akiba imeongezeka kutoka Sh1.114 trilioni mwaka 2023 hadi Sh1.203 trilioni mwaka 2024 na Sh1.310 trilioni mwaka 2025.
Kwa mujibu wa BoT ongezeko hili ni sehemu ya mabadiliko ya namna wananchi wanavyotafuta mahali pa kuweka fedha huku mfumo wa ushirika ukiendelea kuwa kiungo kati ya akiba, mikopo na shughuli za kiuchumi za wanachama.
Saccos zinasimamiwa chini ya Sheria ya Huduma Ndogo za Fedha, 2018 pamoja na Kanuni za Huduma Ndogo za Fedha Vyama vya Ushirika wa Akiba na Mikopo huku msingi wake ukiwa ushirika chini ya Sheria ya Vyama vya Ushirika, 2013 ambayo inafafanua SACCOS kama chama kilichosajiliwa kwa ajili ya kuhamasisha akiba na kutoa mikopo kwa wanachama.
Lakini, mageuzi hayo hayaishii kwenye Saccos pekee kwani vikundi vya akiba navyo vimebadilisha namna wananchi wanavyokusanya fedha.
Kwa mujibu wa BoT, katika kipindi husika, vikundi 76,070 vya akiba na uwekezaji vilikuwa vimeundwa vikiwa na wanachama 1,012,849 ambavyo vilikusanya Sh17.50 bilioni, huku Sh8.90 bilioni zikitolewa kama mikopo kwa wanachama.
Hata hivyo, ukuaji wa SACCOS na vikundi haujaiondoa benki kwenye nafasi yake kwani bado inaongoza kwa thamani ya fedha zilizohifadhiwa.
Hiyo ni baada ya akaunti za akiba benki kufikia milioni 32.8 mwaka 2025 kutoka milioni 29.7 mwaka 2024 na milioni 23.7 mwaka 2023.
Hilo linashuhudiwa wakati ambao thamani ya fedha katika akaunti hizo nayo iliongezeka kutoka Sh6.74 trilioni mwaka 2023 hadi Sh7.71 trilioni mwaka 2024 na Sh9.79 trilioni mwaka 2025.
Nini maana yake
Akizungumza hilo, Meneja wa Saccos ya Mwananchi, Elikunda Materu anasema kuongezeka kwa watu wanaoweka akiba katika Saccos na vikundi kunachangiwa kwa kiasi kikubwa na fursa ya wanachama kupata mikopo kwa urahisi, haraka na kwa masharti nafuu wanapohitaji fedha.
Anasema kuongezeka kwa gharama za maisha pia kumeifanya jamii kutambua umuhimu wa kuwa na akiba ya dharura hali inayochochea ushiriki wao katika vikundi walivyopo.
“Watu wengi wamehamasika kuweka akiba katika Saccos na vikundi kwa sababu akiba huwapa fursa kubwa ya kupata mikopo kwa urahisi, haraka na kwa masharti nafuu wanapokuwa na mahitaji ya kifedha,” anasema.
Anasema baadhi ya wananchi baada ya kupata hasara katika mifumo mbalimbali ya uwekezaji isiyo rasmi wameelekeza fedha zao Saccos wakiamini kuwa mfumo wa ushirika una usimamizi na ufuatiliaji wa taasisi mbalimbali za Serikali.
“Pia kuongezeka kwa elimu ya fedha kupitia taasisi mbalimbali nako kumeongeza uelewa wa wananchi kuhusu umuhimu wa kujenga tabia ya kuweka akiba kwa ajili ya malengo ya baadaye,” anasema.
Maneno yake yaliungwa mkono na Safia Maendeleo ambaye ni mwalimu wa Vicoba na Saccos anayesema ukuaji wa idadi ya wanachama na akiba katika vyama hivyo unaonyesha kuwa wananchi wanaanza kuona umuhimu wa kuweka fedha kwa mfumo unaowapa fursa ya kupata mikopo pale wanapohitaji mtaji.
Anasema tofauti na mtu anayehifadhi fedha bila mpango maalumu, mwanachama hao wanapoweka akiba mara kwa mara hujenga utaratibu unaoweza kuwasaidia kupata mikopo na kuutumia katika shughuli za uzalishaji.
“Unapoweka akiba kwenye Saccos siyo tu kwamba unatenga fedha bali unajenga uwezo wako wa baadaye. Akiba yako inakuwa sehemu ya msingi wa kupata mkopo ambao unaweza kuutumia kuongeza biashara, kulipia elimu au kufanya shughuli nyingine za maendeleo,” anasema.
Anasema mfumo huo pia umeendelea kuwafikia wananchi ambao wanaweza kupata changamoto kutumia huduma za benki kutokana na kipato kisicho na uhakika au kutokuwa na utaratibu wa kuweka fedha mara kwa mara.
Wasemavyo wananchi
Akizungumzia vikundi, Mwajuma Idrisa mkazi wa Ilala Bungoni anasema uwepo wa aina mbalimbali za mikopo inayokidhi mahitaji tofauti ya wanachama huku ikiwa na masharti nafuu ni moja ya kitu kinachowavutia wengi.
“Kuna mikopo kwa ajili ya biashara, elimu na mahitaji mengine hivyo mwanachama anaweza kuchagua huduma inayolingana na lengo lake badala ya kutumia mkopo mmoja kwa kila hitaji ndani ya muda mfupi, hii ni tofauti na benki ambapo watu wanalazimika kusubiri siku kadhaa ili wapate fedha,” anasema.
Pia vikundi hivyo vimekuwa vikitoa nafasi ya kupata huduma za kifedha katika mazingira ambayo anaweza kuyafahamu na kufuatilia kwa urahisi.
“Lakini kabla hujakopa, lazima uwe umeweka akiba ili upate hiyo fursa. Kwa hiyo, siyo tu sehemu ya kupata fedha unapokuwa na uhitaji, bali pia inanifundisha kuwa na utaratibu wa kuweka akiba na kujenga uwezo wa kifedha kwa muda mrefu,” anasema.
Ilivyokua
Haya ni miongoni mwa mageuzi yanayoweza kutajwa katika utunzaji wa akiba kwa wananchi kwani hapo awali asilimia kubwa ya watanzania ilikuwa ikiweka akiba ndani ya nyumba zao badala ya mifumo rasmi ya fedha.
Ripoti ya FinScope Tanzania ya mwaka 2013 ilikuwa ikionyesha kuwa asilimia 65 ya watu waliokuwa wanaweka akiba walihifadhi fedha zao nyumbani, asilimia 21 walitumia huduma za fedha kupitia simu za mkononi, benki zilitumiwa na asilimia 12, vikundi vya akiba asilimia 11 na Saccos asilimia mbili.
Hali hiyo ilianza kubadilika kadri huduma za kifedha zilivyoenea ambapo mwaka 2017, kiwango cha watu walioweka akiba nyumbani kilishuka hadi asilimia 43 huku matumizi ya simu za mkononi yakipanda hadi asilimia 35.
Wakati huo, asilimia 17 ya waliohifadhi akiba walitumia vikundi vya kuweka na kukopa, benki asilimia 16 na asilimia mbili Saccos. FinScope ilibainisha kuwa upatikanaji wa fedha kwa urahisi na usalama wa fedha ni miongoni mwa sababu zilizowafanya watu kuchagua njia hizo.
Hata hivyo, data ya FinScope 2023 zilionyesha kuwa njia zisizo rasmi bado zina nafasi kubwa katika utunzaji wa akiba ambapo asilimia 47 ya Watanzania waliokuwa wanaweka akiba walihifadhi fedha nyumbani, asilimia 34 walitumia simu, asilimia 11 vikundi vya akiba, asilimia 18 benki na asilimia moja Saccos.
Hii ni ishara kuwa pamoja na kuongezeka kwa huduma rasmi na za kidijitali, tabia ya kutunza fedha nyumbani na kutumia mifumo ya kijamii bado ni sehemu muhimu ya maisha ya kifedha ya Watanzania.
Uchumi
Mchumi na mtaalamu wa biashara, Massawe Assey anasema ukuaji wa Saccos na vikundi vya akiba unaonyesha kuwa utunzaji wa fedha unaendelea kutoka kwenye mfumo unaotegemea benki pekee na kuingia katika mifumo inayowafikia zaidi wananchi wenye vyanzo tofauti vya kipato.
“Saccos na vikundi vinapokuwa na uwezo wa kukusanya akiba na kuzigeuza kuwa mikopo, vinasaidia fedha ambazo zingebaki mikononi mwa mtu mmoja kuzunguka ndani ya uchumi kupitia uwekezaji, biashara na shughuli nyingine za uzalishaji,” anasema.
Anasema jambo muhimu siyo tu kuongezeka kwa idadi ya akaunti au thamani ya fedha zilizowekwa bali ni matumizi ya akiba hizo katika kujenga uwezo wa kifedha wa mwananchi.
Anasema mwananchi anapoweka fedha mara kwa mara katika Saccos au kikundi na baadaye kupata mkopo kutokana na akiba hiyo, mfumo huo unaweza kumsaidia kujenga mtaji bila kutegemea vyanzo visivyo rasmi vya fedha.
Anasema pamoja na ukuaji wa Saccos na vikundi vya akiba jambo la kuangalia ni kama ongezeko hilo linaambatana na usalama wa fedha, uwazi na uwezo wa taasisi hizo kuendelea kuwahudumia wanachama.
“Kadri fedha nyingi zinavyoingia kwenye mifumo hiyo ndivyo umuhimu wa usimamizi mzuri, elimu ya fedha na ulinzi wa wanachama unavyoongezeka ili akiba isiwe tu fedha iliyokusanywa, bali iwe rasilimali inayoweza kuwasaidia wananchi kuongeza kipato na kujenga mali,” anasema.

title: Metaller-KV vom Vorjahr bestätigt
content:
Die Arbeitnehmer- und Arbeitgeberseite der Metallindustrie haben den zweiten Teil des im Vorjahr beschlossenen zweijährigen Kollektivvertrages bestätigt. Damit steigen die KV-Löhne 2026/27 um 2,1 Prozent, die Ist-Löhne um 1,9 Prozent – bei einer durchschnittlichen Inflation der vergangenen zwölf Monate (September 2025 bis August 2026) von 3,3 Prozent.
Diese rollierende Inflation ist die Basis für die KV-Verhandlungen, vor zwei Jahren bei der Herbstlohnrunde betrug sie 2,8 Prozent.
Der Mindestlohn in der Metallindustrie liegt somit ab 1. November des heurigen Jahres bei brutto 2.622 Euro. Für die Lehrlinge gibt es ein Plus von 2,1 Prozent, die Zulagen steigen um denselben Wert. Die Zuschläge für Nachtarbeit und die dritte Schicht legen um 7,01 Prozent auf 3,75 Euro pro Stunde zu.
Die Regelung gilt für alle 190.000 Beschäftigten in den sechs Fachverbänden der Metallindustrie. Im Vorjahr gingen 20.000 Stellen in der Metallindustrie verloren, laut Arbeitgebern waren alle Bereiche von der Rezession betroffen. Heuer im August sei aber erstmals wieder Beschäftigung aufgebaut worden.

title: Mifepristone more effective than other common emergency contraception methods
content:
Emergency contraception containing mifepristone prevents more pregnancies with fewer side effects than some other common emergency contraceptive pills, such as levonorgestrel, according to a new review involving 87 trials.
Emergency contraception is used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected sex. It can be used when no contraception was used, if a contraceptive method fails, as with a broken condom, or in the event of sexual assault.
Common methods of emergency contraception include copper intrauterine devices and pills. The most widely used pill is levonorgestrel, a progestin-only medication sold in many countries as "Plan B," "Next Choice" or similar brand names. An alternative is the Yuzpe regimen, an older method that combines estrogen and progestin.
More effective, fewer side effects
The paper, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and led by researchers from Oregon Health & Science University in the United States, pooled data from 87 randomized controlled trials involving approximately 36,000 women of reproductive age. The majority of studies, 79 trials, were conducted in China, with additional trials from the United Kingdom, Cuba and multicountry settings. The authors compared mifepristone with levonorgestrel, the Yuzpe regimen and copper intrauterine devices.
Compared with levonorgestrel, both low-dose (under 25 mg) and mid-dose mifepristone (25–50 mg) prevented more pregnancies and were associated with fewer overall side effects. Low-dose mifepristone showed a 27% relative reduction in pregnancies compared with levonorgestrel. This was rated as high-certainty evidence, meaning further research is very unlikely to change the result.
When compared with the Yuzpe regimen, mifepristone showed an even larger advantage, cutting pregnancy risk substantially while also sharply reducing rates of nausea and vomiting. Evidence comparing mifepristone with copper intrauterine devices remained too limited to draw firm conclusions, based on only two included trials.
"Mifepristone in low-to-mid doses is a highly effective emergency contraceptive option that clinicians should know about," explains Dr. Shaalini Ramanadhan, lead author of the review. "As an antiprogestin, it works differently than the other steroid hormone-based methods like levonorgestrel and combined estrogen and progestin pills to delay or block ovulation. This different mechanism is part of why it has a different side-effect profile compared to the other two methods."
The main trade-off identified across nearly all comparisons was a lower risk of nausea and vomiting with mifepristone but a higher likelihood of delayed menstruation compared with other types of emergency contraception. Given that a delay in menstruation could be interpreted as a sign of treatment failure or pregnancy, the authors explain that this side effect could be a potential source of stress and anxiety for individuals seeking emergency contraception.
Where reported, however, treatment satisfaction was equal to or higher among those who received mifepristone versus alternative methods.
Political and legal barriers limit access
Despite the strong evidence behind the drug's effectiveness as emergency contraception, the authors note that many barriers to access remain.
In some countries, drug authorities have approved mifepristone at higher doses (typically 200 mg) in combination with misoprostol specifically for medical termination of early pregnancy, not as emergency contraception.
Scientific evidence is growing around the potential use of mifepristone and other antiprogestins as a routine method of contraception, for treating fibroids, for preventing and treating breast cancer, and for treating abnormal bleeding. However, because mifepristone is widely associated with abortion, it also faces intense political scrutiny, legal restrictions, and targeted bans and barriers in various countries.
"Expanding options for emergency contraception is important," Ramanadhan says. "The evidence shows that mifepristone has benefits beyond abortion care, including as an effective form of emergency contraception. In some countries, recognition of this additional use may help expand access, increase familiarity with the medication, and create new opportunities for people to benefit from it."

title: Côte d’Ivoire-AIP/ La municipalité de Touba multiplie les investissements pour améliorer le cadre scolaire
content:
Touba, 22 sept 2026 (AIP) – La municipalité de Touba a engagé, depuis 2023, plusieurs actions visant à améliorer le cadre scolaire, notamment à travers la clôture des écoles primaires publiques, la construction et l’extension de salles de classe ainsi que la réhabilitation du Lycée GAF, selon les informations communiquées par le conseil municipal.
Toutes les écoles primaires publiques de la ville sont désormais clôturées, a indiqué la mairie, précisant que cette opération vise à renforcer la sécurité des élèves et des enseignants et à mieux délimiter les espaces scolaires.
La capacité d’accueil des établissements a également été renforcée avec la création ou l’extension de plusieurs écoles, notamment les EPP Dar-Es-Salam, Nadiani 3, Trobiaville, Sekodougou, Dougouba, Municipalité, Plateau 2 et TP Bonisso.
À l’EPP Nadiani 3, la réalisation d’un bâtiment de trois salles de classe a permis de porter la capacité de l’établissement de trois à six classes à la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027. Cette extension doit contribuer à réduire la pression liée aux effectifs dans certaines écoles.
Au secondaire, le Lycée GAF de Touba, présenté comme le seul lycée de la commune, a bénéficié de travaux de réhabilitation et d’aménagement visant à améliorer les conditions d’accueil et de travail des élèves et du personnel éducatif.
Ces interventions répondent notamment à plusieurs insuffisances relevées dans le patrimoine scolaire, dont le déficit de salles de classe, l’absence d’électricité dans certains établissements et la vétusté de bâtiments scolaires au primaire comme au secondaire.
La municipalité accompagne également ces actions par la promotion de l’excellence scolaire. La neuvième édition de la Journée de l’excellence du primaire, organisée le 28 juin 2026 au groupe scolaire Nadiani Mory Fadiga, a permis de récompenser des élèves issus des trois départements de la région du Bafing.
Ces initiatives interviennent dans un contexte marqué par la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027, officiellement lancée le 14 septembre autour du thème « Ensemble, restaurons la confiance pour transformer durablement l’école ».
La municipalité entend poursuivre ses actions en faveur de l’équipement des établissements, de l’amélioration de leur environnement et du bien-être des élèves.
